Where we are

Topic 3 ended on Saturday with the alerts: Lesson 3.5 turned the baseline into rules, severities, notifications and tests, and Lab 2 asks you to configure them on your own MON-01. Topic 4, which starts today, is about the data behind those alerts. An alert is the tool's reading of a few fields; the entries themselves, and the traffic itself, are what a monitoring technician collects and reads when the question "what happened?" arrives. Today covers the two sources that every investigation starts with: the event logs of the Windows and Linux systems (Lesson 4.1) and the capture of network traffic (Lesson 4.2). Tomorrow, Class 14, continues Topic 4 with the next two lessons, on the tools that search and filter what was collected.

What you will be able to do at the end of the hour

These outcomes belong to element 4 of competency EZ01, "Detect and diagnose anomalies", and prepare the performance criterion on the accurate interpretation of the available data.

  1. Read a Windows Security event and a Linux syslog line field by field, and say which field answers which of the six questions: when, where, which source, what, who, from where, with what result.
  2. Recognize the Windows event numbers, logon types and failure reasons that the Class 12 alerts rely on, and find the same information in the Linux authentication log and the journal.
  3. Explain why logs are collected centrally and check a log against the seven conditions that make it trustworthy evidence.
  4. Describe a frame layer by layer, choose a capture point, write a capture filter, bound a capture in size and time, and document it in a capture record.
  5. Read a capture through its summaries: conversations, bytes, timing, services, handshakes, and the names in DNS and TLS.

The running example

We continue with Ébénisterie Val-des-Pins Inc., the fictional cabinet-making workshop of Laval with 22 employees, its Wazuh pilot on MON-01 installed in Lab 2, and the test Monday of Class 12. The timeline above lists what the raw data of that Monday says; every line comes from the examples of this lesson, and by the end of the hour you will know which file each line comes from, which field proves it, and how to collect the same evidence in your lab. The addresses follow the Class 6 plan: office network 10.20.1.0/24 (SRV-FILE-01 at 10.20.1.10, PC-ACCT-01 at 10.20.1.101, MON-01 at 10.20.1.50), workshop 10.20.2.0/24, firewall FW-01 at 10.20.0.1; in your lab replica the same machines are 192.168.56.10, .20 and .21. Everything outside the company uses the address blocks that RFC 5737 reserves for documentation.

Event logs: Windows and Linux

This lesson is folded. Press Unfold lesson 4.1 to show it again.
Slide 5

Part 1: what an event log is

What an event log is, and the six questions it answers

Every operating system, every service and every network device records what it does and what is done to it. One recorded occurrence is an event: a logon, a failed logon, a service that starts, a packet that the firewall refused, a file that was created. The system writes each event as a log entry, and a log entry is a set of fields: the time, the name of the system, the program that wrote the entry, the account concerned, the result. The ordered collection of entries is the event log, or simply the log.

A log entry is useful because it answers questions. There are six of them, and they are the same for every source we will meet today: when did it happen, where (on which system), from which source (which program or channel wrote it), what happened, who was concerned, and from where (which address or workstation), with the result: success or failure, and why. In Class 12 you wrote alert rules that match these fields; today you read the raw entries that the rules were matching. The rules of Class 12 produced the alerts; the entries behind them are the evidence, and the evidence is what Lab 3 asks you to collect, read and report.

Two remarks before we open a log. First, a log records what the system was configured to record, nothing more: an event that the audit policy does not cover never existed in the log. Second, a log is written by the system it describes, so a person who controls that system can also clear or alter the log. Both remarks explain why monitoring collects logs centrally, which is Part 4 of this lesson.

Time: the field that makes two logs comparable

Each entry carries a time stamp, the moment at which the event was recorded. Two entries from two systems can only be put in order if the two clocks agree. Computers keep their clocks in agreement with NTP (Network Time Protocol), published by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) as RFC (Request for Comments) 5905: each system asks a time server for the time at regular intervals and corrects its own clock. In Class 6 we found that FW-01 and SRV-FILE-01 of Val-des-Pins differed by four minutes; until that is corrected, a firewall record at 07:56 and a Windows event at 07:52 may describe the same moment. In Lab 2 you set the time zone of MON-01; in Lab 3 you will check the clocks of all your lab machines before you put their events side by side.

The second part of time is the time zone. Windows stores the time of an event in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) and shows it in the local time of the person who reads it; a Linux syslog file writes the local time of the machine; a packet capture file stores UTC. Montréal is on EDT (Eastern Daylight Time, UTC minus four hours) in October. When you write a timeline, write the time zone once at the top and convert everything to it. A timeline that mixes 06:00 UTC and 02:00 EDT without saying so will describe one event as two.

Part 2: Windows event logs

The Windows event logs

Windows keeps its logs in files with the extension .evtx, under C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs, and shows them in the Event Viewer (the program eventvwr.msc). Each file is a channel, also called a log. Three channels exist on every Windows computer: Application, written by programs; System, written by the operating system and its services; and Security, written by the audit function of Windows. Many other channels exist under "Applications and Services Logs", and some of the most useful for monitoring appear only after a component is installed, such as the Sysmon channel. Table 4.1.A lists the channels that a monitoring technician reads, with the event numbers that come back most often.

Table 4.1.A. Windows event log channels read by a monitoring technician
Channel (log)What it recordsExamples of event numbersMonitoring need it serves (Class 6)
SecurityResults of the audit policy: logons and logoffs, account and group changes, use of administrative privileges, changes to the audit policy, clearing of the log4624, 4625, 4634, 4672, 4720, 4732, 4740, 1102T1 password guessing, T2 privilege change; the source of the Class 12 alerts
SystemThe operating system and its services: a service installed, started or stopped, a driver loaded, a time change, a shutdown, the log service itself7045, 7036, 6005, 6006, 1074, 104T5 device or service outage
ApplicationMessages written by programs: errors, warnings and information from backup software, antivirus, databases1000, vendor-specific numbersT6 backup failure, application errors
Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/OperationalPresent only when Sysmon is installed: process creation with its command line, network connections made by processes, file creation1, 3, 11Detailed endpoint activity; Sysmon is listed among the tools of Topic 4
Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/OperationalDetections, scans and definition updates of the built-in antivirus1116, 1117, 2000T3 malware infection
Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/OperationalScheduled tasks registered, started and completed (disabled by default on workstations)106, 200Planned jobs; unexpected tasks

A Windows event has two parts. The System part is the same for every event: the provider that wrote it, the event number (the field EventID), the level, the time of creation, the record number (EventRecordID, which increases by one with every event written, so a jump in the numbers reveals a gap), and the computer name. The EventData part depends on the event number: event 4625 carries the account name, the logon type, the source address, the workstation name and the reason for the failure; event 4732 carries the group and the member added. The Event Viewer shows the two parts on the "Details" tab, in a "Friendly View" and in XML (Extensible Markup Language). The field names you see in XML are the names that a filter, a script or a Wazuh rule uses.

The Security log: the events to know

The Security log is the main source of the Class 12 alerts, and it is also the log that an intruder clears. Table 4.1.B gives the event numbers that you must recognize on sight. Four families cover most of the monitoring work. The logon events: 4624 for a successful logon, 4625 for a failure, 4634 and 4647 for a logoff, 4648 for a logon made with explicit credentials, for example the runas command. The privilege event 4672, written when an administrative session opens: when you see a 4624 and a 4672 with the same account at the same second, an administrator has just logged on. The account management events: 4720 when an account is created, 4726 when one is deleted, 4732 when a member is added to a local group such as Administrators, 4740 when an account is locked out after too many failures. And the audit integrity events: 1102 when the Security log is cleared, and 4719 when the audit policy itself is changed. In Table 4.1.B each event is linked to the Class 12 alert that uses it, so that the connection between the raw data and the rule is explicit.

Table 4.1.B. Windows Security events to know
EventMeaningFields to readClass 12 alert that uses it

4634An account was logged offTargetUserName, LogonId (pairs with the 4624 of the same session), LogonTypeSession length
4647User initiated logoffTargetUserName, LogonIdSession length

Two fields of the logon events deserve a table of their own. The logon type (Table 4.1.C) tells how the account reached the computer: type 2 is a logon at the keyboard, type 3 a logon over the network, for example when PC-ACCT-01 opens a shared folder of SRV-FILE-01, type 5 a service, type 10 a remote desktop session. The same account logging on with type 2 at 06:42 on the accounting computer and with type 3 at 06:43 on the file server is one person arriving at work; the same account logging on with type 10 at 22:15 is something that the alert AL-03 of Class 12 was written to catch. The SubStatus field of event 4625 (Table 4.1.D) gives the reason of a failure as a hexadecimal code: 0xC000006A is a wrong password, 0xC0000064 an account that does not exist, 0xC0000234 an account that is locked out. The distinction matters: five wrong passwords for one existing account and five attempts on account names that do not exist are two different behaviours, and only the SubStatus field separates them.

What is recorded depends on the audit policy

Windows writes a Security event only if the corresponding audit policy setting is enabled, for success, for failure or for both. A workstation records logon successes and failures by default; a server records more. Some useful events are off until an administrator enables them: event 4688, "a new process has been created", is written only when "Audit Process Creation" is enabled, and its command line field stays empty unless the policy "Include command line in process creation events" is also on. Microsoft publishes the recommended settings in its audit policy recommendations, linked in the links section. You can read the active policy with the command auditpol /get /category:*, and the size and retention of a channel with wevtutil gl Security: a workstation keeps a limited number of megabytes and overwrites the oldest events when the file is full, which is the second reason, after clearing, why a local log is not a complete record.

Reading and exporting Windows events

Three tools read the same channels. The Event Viewer filters a channel by event number, time and account ("Filter Current Log"), and accepts an XML filter for more precise conditions. The command-line tool wevtutil queries and exports channels: wevtutil qe Security /q:"*[System[(EventID=4625)]]" /c:20 /f:text prints the last twenty failures, and wevtutil epl Security C:\exports\security.evtx exports the whole channel to a file that another computer can open. The PowerShell cmdlet Get-WinEvent does the same with filters written as a hashtable, and it can turn each event into a line of a CSV (comma-separated values) file, which is the format that the program of Real-life example 4.1 reads. The export used in the example was produced with the following command, run as an administrator on SRV-FILE-01 (the lines starting with # are comments):

# Export six event numbers of the last two days from the Security log to a CSV file, one event per line.
$ids = 4624,4625,4672,4720,4732,1102
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=$ids; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-2)} |
  ForEach-Object {
    # The XML of the event gives every EventData field by name.
    $x = [xml]$_.ToXml(); $d = @{}
    foreach ($n in $x.Event.EventData.Data) { $d[$n.Name] = $n.'#text' }
    # One object per event, with the columns that the lesson's program expects.
    [pscustomobject]@{ TimeCreated = $_.TimeCreated.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'); EventID = $_.Id; Computer = $env:COMPUTERNAME
      RecordId = $_.RecordId; TargetUserName = $d['TargetUserName']; LogonType = $d['LogonType']; IpAddress = $d['IpAddress']
      WorkstationName = $d['WorkstationName']; SubStatus = $d['SubStatus']; SubjectUserName = $d['SubjectUserName']
      MemberName = $d['MemberName']; Detail = ($_.Message -split "`n")[0] }
  } | Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation -Encoding UTF8 C:\exports\security_export.csv

Two details of this export are worth remembering. In event 4732 the member added to the group is often given only as a SID (security identifier, the text S-1-5-21-...), in the field MemberSid; the name must be resolved from it, which the example file has already done. And the Computer field is the name of the host that wrote the event, not the host that caused it: the source of a network logon is in IpAddress and WorkstationName.

Part 3: Linux logs

Linux logs: the syslog standard

Linux programs write their messages through syslog, a standard defined by the IETF in RFC 5424 (the older, simpler format is described in RFC 3164). Every message carries a facility, which says where it comes from (the kernel, the mail system, the authentication functions, a local use reserved for devices such as FW-01), and a severity from 0, Emergency, to 7, Debug, the scale you met in Class 12 (Table 3.5.I). The two numbers are combined into the priority value written at the start of a message when it travels over the network: facility times eight, plus severity. A line sent by the authentication facility with the severity Informational starts with <38>, because 4 times 8 is 32, plus 6. Table 4.1.F lists the facilities.

Table 4.1.F. Syslog facilities (RFC 5424): the origin of a message
NumberFacilityMessages from
0kernThe kernel
1userUser-level programs
2mailThe mail system
3daemonSystem daemons
4authSecurity and authorization (logins)
5syslogThe syslog daemon itself
6lprPrinting
7newsNetwork news
8uucpUUCP (Unix-to-Unix Copy)
9cronThe scheduler
10authprivSecurity and authorization, private (sudo, PAM)
11ftpFTP (File Transfer Protocol) daemon
12ntpTime synchronization
13securityLog audit
14consoleLog alert
15solaris-cronScheduling daemon
16 to 23local0 to local7Local use: FW-01 and SW-01 send their syslog messages with one of these
The priority value at the start of a syslog message is facility x 8 + severity: <38> is auth (4 x 8 = 32) plus informational (6). The severities are in Table 3.5.I of Class 12.

On Ubuntu Server 24.04, the version installed on MON-01 in Lab 2, the program that receives these messages and writes them to files is rsyslog. A line in a file has four parts, visible in Figure 4.1.1: the time stamp, the host name, the program name with its process number in square brackets, and the message. The traditional time stamp, "Oct 5 07:49:04", has no year and no time zone; newer rsyslog configurations can write the full ISO 8601 form, "2026-10-05T07:49:04.123456-04:00", which has both. A script that reads a log must accept both, which is why the program of Real-life example 4.1 locates the fields by the text around them rather than by their position. The message part is free text written by the program: OpenSSH writes "Failed password for invalid user admin from 10.20.1.104 port 51522 ssh2"; the sudo program writes the user, the terminal, the directory and the command; PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules), the component that checks passwords for all these programs, writes "session opened for user tech(uid=1000)". The field names are not written in the line: you must know the message formats of the programs you monitor, and the documentation of each program gives them.

Where the files are, and the journal

Table 4.1.E lists the files under /var/log that a monitoring technician reads on MON-01. The authentication log, /var/log/auth.log on Ubuntu and Debian (/var/log/secure on Red Hat systems), holds the SSH (Secure Shell) logins and failures, the sudo commands and the PAM sessions: it is the Linux counterpart of the Windows Security log. The general log /var/log/syslog holds everything else, including the messages of the Wazuh manager; /var/log/kern.log holds the kernel messages, including the host firewall decisions. Three files are not text: wtmp, btmp and lastlog record the sessions opened, the failed logins and the last login of each user in a binary format, read with the commands last, lastb and lastlog. The files are owned by the user syslog and the group adm, and only members of that group, or sudo, can read them: a log that everybody can read would expose the personal information it contains.

Table 4.1.E. Where the Linux logs are (Ubuntu Server 24.04 on MON-01)
File or storeWritten byWhat it containsHow to read it
/var/log/auth.logrsyslog (facilities auth and authpriv)SSH (Secure Shell) logins and failures, sudo commands, PAM sessions, cron sessions, user and group changessudo grep sshd /var/log/auth.log; sudo tail -f /var/log/auth.log
/var/log/syslogrsyslog (all facilities)Everything the system and the daemons write, including the Wazuh manager messagessudo grep wazuh /var/log/syslog
/var/log/kern.logrsyslog (facility kern)Kernel messages: network interfaces up and down, disk errors, firewall (ufw) decisionssudo grep -i ufw /var/log/kern.log
/var/log/ufw.logrsyslog (ufw messages)Blocked and allowed packets of the host firewall, when logging is onsudo tail /var/log/ufw.log
/var/log/dpkg.log and /var/log/apt/history.logdpkg and aptPackages installed, upgraded and removed (the update log of Lab 2, Criterion 3.3)grep upgrade /var/log/apt/history.log
/var/log/wtmp, /var/log/btmp, /var/log/lastloglogin, sshd (binary files)Sessions opened (wtmp), failed logins (btmp), last login per user (lastlog)last; sudo lastb; lastlog
/var/log/journal/ (the journal)systemd-journaldEvery message of every service, with structured fields, from boot to bootjournalctl -u ssh --since "2026-10-05 07:00"
/var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.json and archives/archives.jsonWazuh managerThe alerts (always) and every event received (when logall_json is enabled): the central copy of the other hosts' logssudo tail -n 200 /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.json
/var/log/*.1, *.2.gzlogrotateThe rotated and compressed older copies (weekly rotation, a limited number kept)zgrep sshd /var/log/auth.log.2.gz

Since the adoption of systemd, Linux also keeps the journal: a binary, indexed store written by systemd-journald, which receives every message of every service, with structured fields (the unit, the process, the priority, the boot). The command journalctl reads it with filters: journalctl -u ssh --since "2026-10-05 07:00" --until "2026-10-05 09:00" shows the SSH service between two times, journalctl -p err -b the errors since the last boot, journalctl -o json the entries as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) objects that a program can read. On Ubuntu 24.04 the journal and the rsyslog files coexist: the journal receives everything first and rsyslog writes the files from it. The files are rotated by logrotate: every week the current file is renamed with the suffix .1, the older ones are compressed (.2.gz, .3.gz) and the oldest is deleted, so a file keeps a few weeks at most. That limit is the Linux version of the Windows log size: local retention is short, central retention is the one that counts.

Reading Linux logs

Four commands do most of the reading. grep keeps the lines that match a pattern: sudo grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log. awk extracts fields from each line and prints them in the order you choose. sort and uniq -c count the repeats: a list of source addresses becomes a table of how many failures came from each. tail -f follows a file while it grows, which is how you watch a test in Lab 3 as it happens. The program of Real-life example 4.1 uses exactly these commands, and its comments explain each one. For a structured search, journalctl and its JSON output replace all four. When the question is "which accounts and which sources", the method is the same on both systems: filter the entries, extract the fields of the common schema, count, and put the result in time order.

Part 4: collecting centrally

Why the logs are collected centrally

At 07:58:40 on the test Monday, the Security log of SRV-FILE-01 was cleared by the account admin.it. On SRV-FILE-01 the log now starts with event 1102, record number 1, and the thirteen events of the morning are gone. They exist only because the Wazuh agent installed in Lab 2 had already sent each event to MON-01 as it was written. Central collection is the practice of copying every log entry to a system that the monitored hosts cannot modify, as soon as the entry is written. It serves three purposes: the copy survives the clearing, the filling and the failure of the local log; the entries of all the hosts can be searched together, in one place and in one format; and the retention, the period during which entries are kept, is decided by the monitoring plan, not by the size of a local file. At Val-des-Pins the constraint C-03 of Class 6 fixes it at 90 days, the minimum that safeguard 8.10 of the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls recommends; the CCCS (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security) says the same in its guidance on network security logging and monitoring, and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) describes the whole practice in its SP (Special Publication) 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management.

Figure 4.1.3 shows the collection paths configured in Lab 2. The Wazuh agent on each Windows host reads the Security, System and Application channels through the Windows event log interface (the log format called eventchannel in the agent configuration) and sends them to the manager on port 1514 over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol). On MON-01 the local agent reads the files of Table 4.1.E and the journal. FW-01 and SW-01 cannot run an agent: they send their messages with the syslog protocol, over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 514, to the manager, which accepts remote syslog connections. UDP syslog has no encryption and no acknowledgement; a device that supports it should use syslog over TLS (Transport Layer Security), RFC 5425, port 6514. The manager decodes each entry into fields, evaluates the rules, writes the alerts to alerts.json and, when the option logall_json is enabled, every received entry to archives.json: that archive is the central copy from which the example data of today was exported.

The common schema

A Windows event and a syslog line do not have the same fields, and the firewall records have a third set. Before entries from several sources can be compared, each one is translated into a common schema: one fixed list of fields with one meaning each, filled from whatever the source provides. This translation is called normalization. Table 4.1.G gives the schema used in this course: time with its zone, host, source, event, outcome, account, source address, detail. Monitoring tools do this translation with decoders, which you wrote in Lab 2 for the volume lines of the firewall; the programs of today do it in a few lines of Python and bash. Once the entries share a schema, the questions of a diagnosis become operations on a table: sort by time, group by account, count by source address.

Table 4.1.G. The common schema: one set of fields for every event, whatever its source
FieldMeaningWindows Security eventLinux syslog lineCapture (Lesson 4.2)
timeWhen the event happened, with its time zoneTimeCreated (stored in UTC, shown in local time)The time stamp at the start of the line (local time; no year in the traditional format)Packet time stamp (UTC in the file)
hostThe system that recorded the eventComputerThe host name after the time stampThe capturing interface (MON-01)
sourceThe program or channel that wrote itChannel and Provider (Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing)program[pid] (sshd[2231], sudo, CRON)Protocol decoded (DNS, TCP, TLS)
eventWhat happenedEventID (4625)The message text (Failed password for ...)Flags and message types (SYN, query, ClientHello)
outcomeSuccess or failure, and why4624 or 4625; SubStatusAccepted or Failed; invalid userHandshake completed, reset, no answer
accountWhoTargetUserName, SubjectUserNameThe user name in the messageNot visible (addresses only)
source addressFrom whereIpAddress, WorkstationNamefrom 10.20.1.104 port 51522Source address and port
detailAnything else needed to understand itLogonType, PrivilegeList, MemberNameMethod (publickey, password), command (sudo)Bytes, DNS name, TLS server name

Seven checks before trusting a log

An entry is evidence only if the log it comes from can be trusted. Table 4.1.H lists seven checks, and the Lab 3 report has a section for them: the clock and the time zone, the coverage of the audit policy, the completeness (no gaps, no cleared log, no silent source), the integrity (who could modify it), the retention, the access (who can read it), and the format (which version of which tool wrote it). The checks are short to perform and long to regret when they are skipped.

Table 4.1.H. Seven checks before trusting a log
CheckQuestionHow to verify at Val-des-PinsWhat goes wrong otherwise
1. ClockIs the clock of the source synchronized (NTP) and is the time zone known?timedatectl on MON-01; w32tm /query /status on Windows; compare with FW-01 (4-minute difference found in Class 6)Events from two systems cannot be put in order
2. CoverageDoes the audit policy record what the monitoring need requires?auditpol /get /category:* on Windows; rsyslog configuration on LinuxThe event never existed: nothing to find
3. CompletenessAre there gaps: cleared logs, a full log that overwrote old events, a silent source?Event 1102 and 104; wevtutil gl Security (size); AL-09 of Class 12A gap read as 'nothing happened'
4. IntegrityCan the log be modified by the people it describes?Local administrators can clear a local log; the central copy on MON-01 cannot be cleared from the hostEvidence lost or altered
5. RetentionHow long are the events kept, locally and centrally?Local: the log size; central: 90 days (constraint C-03, CIS safeguard 8.10)The event is gone when the question is asked
6. AccessWho can read the log?adm group and sudo on Linux; Event Log Readers group on Windows; dashboard accounts on MON-01Personal information read by people who have no need
7. FormatIs the format known and stable (time stamp format, field names, version of the tool)?Document the version of rsyslog, of Windows and of the Wazuh agentA parsing script silently reads the wrong field

Logs are personal information. A log entry names a person's account, the time of their work and the address of their computer. Under Québec's Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, as amended by Law 25, and under PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) federally, such records are personal information: collect the minimum, protect it, give access only to the people who need it, and delete it when it is no longer needed. In this course the rule is written in section 7.2 of the Legal Notice: every log file, baseline and alert record of the lab is treated as personal information, stays in the lab, and is deleted when the exercise is marked. The same section forbids installing a collector or an agent on any device that is not yours or a Designated Target.

Real-life example 4.1: the raw entries behind the Monday alerts, on Windows and on Linux

Task

Collect the raw entries behind the Class 12 alerts of the test Monday from two operating systems: export the Windows Security events of SRV-FILE-01 and PC-ACCT-01 (the local log and the central copy on MON-01), read the authentication log of MON-01, decode the fields, merge everything into one evidence timeline with a per-account and a per-source summary, and note what the cleared log did to the local evidence.

Link with the lecture

The example applies the six questions of a log entry, the Windows event numbers, logon types and failure reasons of Tables 4.1.B to 4.1.D, the syslog line format and the Linux files of Table 4.1.E, the common schema of Table 4.1.G and the checks of Table 4.1.H. Its two outputs are the evidence section of the Lab 3 anomaly report.

On Tuesday morning the monitoring technician of Val-des-Pins has the eight alerts of the Monday on the Wazuh dashboard and one question from the owner: what happened? Alerts are not evidence; they are the tool's reading of the evidence. The technician starts by collecting the entries themselves, from three places.

The Windows hosts. On SRV-FILE-01 the PowerShell export of Part 2 produces a file of nine events only: the local log begins at 07:58:40 with event 1102, because it was cleared. On MON-01 the archive of the Wazuh manager still has every event received from both Windows hosts since the agents were installed; exported with the same columns, it gives 24 events for the Monday. Both files are read by the Python program of Code example 4.1.A, which decodes the event numbers, the logon types and the SubStatus codes, merges the two copies without counting an event twice, and prints the timeline you see in Figure 4.1.2: the clerk's logon at 06:42 (type 2, before 07:00, which raised AL-03), one failure and one success of shop.lead at 07:40 (a typo), five failures of admin.it from 10.20.1.104 between 07:52:01 and 07:53:12, all with the reason "wrong password" (AL-01), the success at 07:54:30 followed in the same second by event 4672 (AL-02, and an administrative session), the creation of svc.backup2 at 07:55:50 and its addition to Administrators at 07:56:05 (AL-04), the clearing at 07:58:40 (AL-05), and the clerk's five failures at 10:13 when a new password was mistyped, followed by a success.

The Linux host. Was MON-01 touched? Its authentication log, read by the bash program of Code example 4.1.B, shows eight SSH failures between 07:49:04 and 07:50:10 from the same address 10.20.1.104: three for the account "admin", which does not exist on MON-01, three for "administrator", which does not exist either, and two for root. Then nothing until 08:05, when the technician's own key-based login appears, followed by two sudo commands used to read the alerts. The failures on MON-01 come three minutes before the failures on SRV-FILE-01, from the same source, with account names that exist on neither system: this is what the two logs say when they are read together, and the program says nothing more. The diagnosis, which account names, which workstation, which person, belongs to Lab 3 and to Topic 5.

The checks. Before writing anything, the technician applies Table 4.1.H: MON-01 and the Windows hosts are synchronized with NTP since Lab 2 (clock); the audit policy records logon success and failure, account management and privilege use (coverage); the local log of SRV-FILE-01 has a gap from the start of the day to 07:58:40 and the central copy has none (completeness); the account that cleared the log is a local administrator of SRV-FILE-01 and has no access to MON-01 (integrity); 90 days of retention on MON-01 (retention); the exports are stored in the lab folder of the case, readable by the technician only (access); the Windows export was made with Get-WinEvent on Windows 11 and the Linux log by rsyslog 8.x, the version printed by rsyslogd -v (format).

Deliverables and the lab they feed

  • Deliverable 1, the evidence timeline (class13_evidence_timeline_output.csv, 24 rows) and the per-account summary printed by Code 4.1.A. In Lab 3 the same program, run on your own exports, produces the evidence section of your anomaly report.
  • Deliverable 2, the authentication summary of MON-01 (class13_mon_01_auth_summary_output.csv, 11 rows) printed by Code 4.1.B, with the count of failures per source. In Lab 3 it answers the question "was the monitoring server itself a target?" for your lab.

          4.2
          Network traffic capture: the basics
          This lesson is folded. Press Unfold lesson 4.2 to show it again.
          Slide 31
          Part 1: packets, frames and headers
          

          Packets, frames and headers
          

          A log is written by the system that acts; a network traffic capture is a copy of what travelled on the wire, made by an observer that the acting system does not control. The two sources answer different questions, and the Lab 3 investigation needs both: the logs say which account did what on which host; the capture says what left the host, to which destination, how much and when.
          

          Data travels on a network in packets: units of limited size, each carrying a part of the data and the information needed to deliver it. On an Ethernet network the unit that the capture tool sees is the frame, at most 1514 bytes without the check sequence. A frame is built in layers, and each layer adds a header, a fixed set of fields placed in front of the data it carries; the data carried is the payload. This nesting is called encapsulation, and Figure 4.2.1 shows it for one frame of the night upload: 14 bytes of Ethernet header (the MAC (Media Access Control) addresses of the sending and receiving interfaces on the local network and the type of the next layer), 20 bytes of IP (Internet Protocol) header, version 4 (the source and destination addresses, the protocol of the next layer, the length, the TTL (time to live)), 20 bytes of TCP header (the source and destination ports, the sequence and acknowledgement numbers, the flags SYN, ACK, FIN, RST and PSH, the window), and then the payload, here a TLS record of 1460 bytes. UDP, used by DNS (Domain Name System), NTP and syslog, replaces the TCP header by an 8-byte header with the ports and the length. Table 4.2.D lists, layer by layer, the fields that answer the monitoring questions and where each one appears in the sample capture.
          Table 4.2.D. Header fields that answer the monitoring questions
          LayerHeaderFields that matterQuestion answeredIn the sample capture
          2Ethernet (14 bytes)Destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType (0x0800 IPv4, 0x0806 ARP, 0x86DD IPv6)Which device on the local network sent the frame02:00:10:20:01:65 is PC-ACCT-01; frames to the Internet carry the MAC of FW-01
          3IPv4 (20 bytes without options)Source address, destination address, protocol (6 TCP, 17 UDP, 1 ICMP: Internet Control Message Protocol), total length, TTL, identificationWho talks to whom, how much10.20.1.101 to 203.0.113.50, protocol 6
          4TCP (20 bytes without options)Source port, destination port, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH), windowWhich service, how the connection opened and closed, how much data49731 to 443; SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK at 01:59:59
          4UDP (8 bytes)Source port, destination port, lengthWhich service (53 DNS, 123 NTP, 514 syslog)53444 to 53; 123 to 123
          7DNS (over UDP 53)Transaction id, flags (query or response), question name, answers (name, type, TTL, address)Which name the client asked for, which address it receivedupload.example.net = 203.0.113.50, TTL 300
          7TLS record and ClientHello (over TCP 443)Record type (22 handshake, 23 application data), version, the server name extension (SNI) in the ClientHelloWhich server name the client wanted; the content itself stays encryptedSNI upload.example.net in frame 25 of the sample
          7Application data (TLS type 23)Only the length and the timingHow much and when; not what1455-byte records, 89 per second
          

          Two application protocols are read in this lesson because their headers carry names. A DNS exchange is a query and a response over UDP port 53: the query holds the name that the client asked for, the response holds the addresses that answer it and a TTL that says how long the client may keep the answer. A TLS session starts with a ClientHello message, which carries the SNI (Server Name Indication) extension: the name of the server that the client wants, in clear text, before the encryption starts. Everything after the handshake is encrypted: the capture shows records of type 23, "application data", with their lengths and their timing, and nothing else. This is the limit of a capture of encrypted traffic, and also its remaining value: who, with whom, which service, which name, how much, when, and how the connection opened and closed are all visible; the content and the account are not.
          

          Slide 34
          Part 2: where and how to capture
          

          Where to capture: the capture point
          

          A capture tool reads the frames that reach one network interface. The question "where" is therefore the question of which interface sees the traffic you need, and Table 4.2.A compares the possibilities. Capturing on the host itself is the simplest and the worst for an investigation: the person who uses the computer can see, stop or alter the capture, and a computer that may be compromised is not a trustworthy observer. A managed switch offers a mirror port, also called a SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) port: the switch copies the frames of one or several ports to a monitoring port, where the capture host listens; SW-01 of Val-des-Pins supports it, the unmanaged SW-02 of the workshop does not. A network TAP (test access point) is a device inserted in a link that copies the signal to monitoring outputs; it sees every bit at full speed but inserting it interrupts the link for a moment. In the laboratory there is no physical switch, so the lab stand-in is the VirtualBox host-only network: when the adapter of MON-01 is set to promiscuous mode (Settings, Network, Adapter 2, Advanced, Promiscuous Mode: Allow All), the interface accepts every frame on the host-only network and not only the frames addressed to it, which is what a mirror port would deliver. This is how Lab 3 captures the traffic of PC-ACCT-01 on MON-01.
          Table 4.2.A. Where to capture: the capture points
          Capture pointHow it worksSeesDoes not seeVal-des-Pins / lab
          On the host itselfThe capture tool runs on the computer being watched (tcpdump, dumpcap)Everything that enters and leaves that computer's interfaceOther hosts; and the host's owner can see or stop the captureNot on PC-ACCT-01: the person using it must not be able to alter the evidence; used on MON-01 for its own traffic
          Mirror port (SPAN)The managed switch copies the frames of chosen ports to a monitoring portAll the traffic of the mirrored ports, without touching the production linkTraffic of an unmanaged switch; frames dropped when the mirror port is saturatedSW-01 supports it; SW-02 (workshop) does not
          Network TAPA device inserted in a link copies the signal to monitoring outputsEvery bit of the link, at full speedOnly that link; inserting it means a short interruptionPossible on the FW-01 link; not needed for this investigation
          Promiscuous adapter in the labThe VirtualBox host-only adapter of MON-01 set to Promiscuous Mode: Allow AllAll the frames of the host-only network 192.168.56.0/24Nothing outside the labThe lab stand-in for the SPAN port (Lab 3)
          Flow records (not a capture)FW-01 exports one record per connection: addresses, ports, bytes, durationWho talked to whom, how much, whenThe content of the packets, the DNS names, the handshake detailsActivity A5b of Class 6, accepted; the capture is the targeted complement
          

          At Val-des-Pins, Class 6 rejected activity A5, a full capture of the Internet link: 30 megabits per second, 324 gigabytes per day, about 29,000 gigabytes over 90 days, 24 times the capacity of NAS-01. The accepted alternative, A5b, is the export of flow records by FW-01: one record per connection with the addresses, the ports, the bytes and the duration, which answers "who, with whom, how much, when" for 37 gigabytes over 90 days. A capture is therefore not a permanent source at a small company; it is a targeted source, started for one host and one question, for a bounded time, and stopped. Table 4.2.F puts the four options side by side with their arithmetic.
          Table 4.2.F. Storage arithmetic: full capture, headers only, flow records (90 days, Class 6 figures)
          MethodVolume per secondPer dayOver 90 daysDecision
          Full packet capture of the Internet link (A5)30 Mbit/s = 3.75 MB/s324 GBabout 29,000 GBRejected in Class 6: 24 times the NAS
          Flow records from FW-01 (A5b)40 records/s x 120 bytes = 4.8 kB/s0.41 GB37 GBAccepted: who, with whom, how much, when
          Targeted capture of one host, full frames135 kB/s during the upload0.49 GB per hour of uploadBounded by the capture windowLab 3 investigation, one night
          Targeted capture of one host, snapshot 256 bytesabout 23 kB/s during the upload (256 of 1514 bytes)0.08 GB per hour of uploadBounded by the capture windowThe plan of Real-life example 4.2
          Rule: bytes per second x 86,400 seconds x retention days. 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes.
          

          The tools and the file format
          

          All the usual capture tools rest on the same library, libpcap (on Windows, Npcap). tcpdump is the command-line tool of Linux servers such as MON-01, which has no graphical display; Wireshark is the graphical analyser, with its own command-line capture tool, dumpcap, and its text analyser, tshark. The usual method is therefore to capture with tcpdump on MON-01, to copy the file to a computer with Wireshark, and to read it there. The file format written by tcpdump is pcap (packet capture): a 24-byte global header (a magic number, the version, the snapshot length and the link type), then one record per frame with the time stamp in UTC, the number of bytes kept and the number of bytes that were on the wire. Wireshark saves by default in the newer pcapng format, which adds comments, several interfaces and name resolution blocks; the two are documented by the IETF, and the command editcap -F pcap converts a pcapng file to pcap when a tool, such as the program of today, reads only the older format.
          

          Four options of tcpdump shape a capture, and Table 4.2.B gives them all. The capture filter is written in the pcap-filter language, documented in the manual pcap-filter(7): host 10.20.1.101 and not port 514 keeps the frames of PC-ACCT-01 and drops the syslog traffic to MON-01. A capture filter decides what is written to the disk, so it cannot be undone; a display filter in Wireshark, such as tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0, only decides what is shown and can be changed at any time; Table 4.2.C puts the two languages side by side. The snapshot length (option -s) is the number of bytes of each frame that are kept: 256 bytes keep every header and the server name of a ClientHello, and leave most of the content out, which reduces the file size and the personal information collected at the same time; with a short snapshot length the byte counts must be read from the original length recorded in each record, not from the bytes kept. The option -n stops name resolution, so that the capture host does not itself send DNS queries while it observes. And the options -G and -W bound the capture in time: one file per hour, and a stop after a chosen number of files, so that a capture started at night cannot fill the disk by Monday; the alternative -C with -W rotates files by size for a longer, continuous buffer.

          The capture record and the legal frame
          

          A capture that cannot be explained is not evidence. Table 4.2.E lists the capture record: the authorization that permitted it, the operator and the start time in UTC and local time, the capture point and the interface, the filter and the snapshot length, the tool and its version, the files with their sizes and their SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256 bits) hashes, the stop time and the reason, the storage location and the deletion date. The hash proves later that the file analysed is the file captured; the program of Code example 4.2.A writes this record for you.

          Capturing is interception. Section 184 of the Criminal Code of Canada makes it an offence to knowingly intercept a private communication, and capturing other people's traffic on a network you share with them is interception, whatever the intention. Section 7.2 of the Legal Notice applies it to this course: capture only on interfaces of systems you own or that are Designated Targets, only for the duration of the exercise, never in promiscuous mode on a network shared with other people (home, residence, campus, workplace), and treat every capture file as personal information. At Val-des-Pins the guest Wi-Fi is excluded from every capture and every log by constraint C-05, and the capture of Real-life example 4.2 is limited to one host, by filter, for one night, with a written reference to its authorization. The same tool used on the college network would be an offence under section 342.1 as well; section 6.3 lists it among the prohibited activities.
          

          Slide 41
          Part 3: reading a capture
          

          Reading a capture: five questions, in this order
          

          A capture of a few seconds holds hundreds of frames; reading them one by one is the last step, not the first. Start with the questions that summaries answer. Who talks with whom? A conversation is the set of frames exchanged between two endpoints, identified by the two addresses, the two ports and the protocol; Wireshark lists them under Statistics, Conversations, and the program of Code example 4.2.B builds the same table. How much? The bytes in each direction, from which the top talkers are ranked; a workstation that sends more than it receives is unusual, because a workstation normally downloads. When? The time column of the frames, and the bytes per second: Wireshark's Statistics, I/O Graphs, or the per-second list of the program. Which service? The destination port, the DNS name that the client asked for just before, and the server name of the ClientHello. How did it start and end? The three-way handshake (SYN from the client, SYN and ACK from the server, ACK from the client) shows that the connection was opened normally by a program on the client; a FIN closes it, a RST aborts it; a SYN with no answer is a connection attempt that failed. Only after these five answers does it make sense to open individual frames.
          

          In Wireshark, the display filters of Table 4.2.C give the same answers on the sample capture of today: dns shows the two lookups, tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 the two connection openings, tls.handshake.extensions_server_name the two server names announced, and tcp.stream eq 1 the whole upload conversation. The Protocol Hierarchy under Statistics shows what share of the bytes belongs to each protocol, which is the fastest way to see that one conversation dominates a capture.
          

          One question that a capture does not answer: which program on the host sent the traffic. That answer is on the host, in event 4688 with its command line, or in the Sysmon network connection event (number 3), which records the process name with the destination address and port. The two lessons of today meet exactly there: the capture gives the destination, the volume and the time; the host log gives the process and the account. Lab 3 asks for both.

          Slide 44
          Real-life example 4.2: what left PC-ACCT-01 at 02:00?
          

          Task
          Plan an authorized capture of the traffic of PC-ACCT-01 for the night that follows the alerts (on MON-01, through the mirror port of SW-01 at the company and through the promiscuous host-only adapter in the lab), with a capture filter, a snapshot length, timed files and a capture record; then read the capture to answer the question left open since Class 12: what left PC-ACCT-01 at 02:00?
          

          Link with the lecture
          The example applies the capture points of Table 4.2.A, the tcpdump options of Table 4.2.B, the two filter languages of Table 4.2.C, the header fields of Table 4.2.D, the capture record of Table 4.2.E and the storage arithmetic of Table 4.2.F. Its two outputs are the method section and part of the evidence section of the Lab 3 anomaly report.
          

          The two AL-07 alerts of the Monday said that PC-ACCT-01 sent 486 and 512 megabytes to the Internet at 02:00 and 03:00, from the firewall's volume lines. The firewall records give the destination address and the bytes, but not the name that was looked up, not the way the connection opened, and not the rate second by second. The technician decides to capture the traffic of that one host during the following night, in case the transfer repeats.
          

          The plan. Capture point: the mirror port of SW-01 (port 7, PC-ACCT-01, copied to port 24, MON-01); in the lab, the host-only adapter of MON-01 in promiscuous mode. Filter: host 10.20.1.101 and not port 514. Snapshot length: 256 bytes, enough for every header and for the TLS server name, not enough for content. Files: one per hour, a stop after eight files, under /captures on MON-01, owned by the user tech. Authorization: the Lab 3 guide names PC-ACCT-01 as a Designated Target, and the technician's Annex A is signed; at a real company the owner's written authorization would be referenced instead (Annex D). The bash program of Code example 4.2.A checks the interface, the tool and the free space, prints the exact command, and appends one line to the capture record with the SHA-256 hash of the first file. Nothing is captured without the option --run, and in this lesson the program runs in its dry mode, which is what you will see in the player.
          

          The capture. The transfer repeated at 02:00. The sample file of today, class13_pc_acct_01_night_sample.pcap, holds its first 35 seconds, 700 frames, generated for the lesson by the program class13_make_sample_pcap.py so that no real network was touched. Read by the Python program of Code example 4.2.B, it shows: an NTP exchange with MON-01 at 01:59:30; at 01:59:57 a DNS lookup of update.example.com, answered 198.51.100.20 with a TTL of one hour, followed by a short TLS session of 13 frames (the vendor update check, on the allowlist of Class 12); at 01:59:58 a DNS lookup of upload.example.net, answered 203.0.113.50 with a TTL of five minutes; at 01:59:59 a complete three-way handshake from port 49731 to port 443, a ClientHello announcing the server name upload.example.net, and from 02:00:00 a continuous stream of 1514-byte frames, 89 per second, acknowledged by the server: 135 kilobytes per second, which is 486 megabytes per hour, the figure of AL-07, against a night threshold of 25.
          

          What the capture says and does not say. It says that PC-ACCT-01 opened the connection itself, after resolving a name, to a server that is not on the vendor list, at a rate that fills the hour, with encrypted content. It does not say which program did it or under which account: for that, the technician returns to the host logs of Lesson 4.1, to event 4688 or to the Sysmon network connection event, which Lab 3 will add to the Lab 2 collection. The conversation table, the DNS answers, the handshake list and the per-second rate are written to the evidence section as they are; the interpretation goes to the diagnosis section, with the limits stated.

                  Step-by-step explanation
                  1. The header states the task, the link with the lecture and how to run the program. Each code line is preceded by a comment line.
                  2. The imports: struct decodes the fixed binary headers, sys reads the optional file name, csv writes the table, datetime and timezone convert the UTC time stamps of the file to the local time of the lab (EDT, UTC minus four hours), and defaultdict creates counters on first use.
                  3. The settings name the capture file, the output file, the host investigated (10.20.1.101), the local time zone and the names of the well-known ports met in the lesson.
                  4. Four helpers: find_file() locates the capture; ip_text() turns four bytes into dotted decimal; dns_name() reads a DNS name, following the compression pointers of the DNS format; dns_answers() returns the A records of a response; tls_server_name() walks a ClientHello to the server name extension and returns the name, or None when the message is something else or was cut by the snapshot length.
                  5. Step 1 reads the 24-byte global header of the file: the magic number (little-endian, microsecond time stamps; anything else stops with a hint), the version 2.4, the snapshot length 256 and the link type 1 (Ethernet). These four facts belong in the capture record.
                  6. Step 2 walks the records. Each 16-byte record header gives the time stamp, the bytes kept and the bytes on the wire; when they differ, the frame was cut by the snapshot length (453 of the 700 frames). The Ethernet type separates ARP (counted), IPv4 (decoded) and the rest. For IPv4 the program reads the header length, the protocol and the two addresses, then the TCP ports, sequence numbers and flags, or the UDP ports.
                  7. Inside the loop, three detectors run: the handshake tracker records SYN, then SYN-ACK, then ACK for each connection attempt; the TLS detector extracts the server name from a ClientHello sent to port 443; the DNS detector stores the name behind each address answered on port 53.
                  8. Still inside the loop, the conversation table is updated: the key puts the two endpoints in a fixed order so that both directions share one entry; the packet count and the wire bytes are added in the right direction; the bytes sent by the target are also added to the per-second counter. The player condenses the 700 iterations and shows one step every 50 frames.
                  9. Step 3 prints the report: the duration and the local times (01:59:30 to 02:00:04 EDT), the frame types, the DNS answers (update.example.com and upload.example.net with their TTLs), the two handshakes (both open), the two server names announced, the conversation table ranked by bytes (the upload conversation first: 703 frames, 675,712 bytes sent), the bytes per second (89 full frames per second from +30 s), and the projection: 135 kB/s, 486 MB per hour, against the AL-07 night threshold of 25 MB.
                  10. Step 4 writes the conversation table to class13_conversations_output.csv, with the DNS name of each destination when one was seen, and prints where it went.
                  To run it, keep class13_pc_acct_01_night_sample.pcap next to the script and type python3 class13_pcap_conversations.py; give another file name to read your own capture (pcap format, Ethernet frames; convert a pcapng file first with editcap -F pcap). Python 3.8 or later, no extra package. The same file opens in Wireshark for the filters of Table 4.2.C.

Slide 52


                  What to remember
                  1. A log entry answers six questions (when, where, which source, what, who, from where, with what result); the fields that answer them differ by source, the questions do not.
                  2. On Windows, the Security channel with its event numbers (4624, 4625, 4672, 4720, 4732, 1102), logon types and SubStatus codes is the evidence behind the Class 12 alerts; what it records depends on the audit policy, and a local log can be cleared or overwritten.
                  3. On Linux, syslog lines (time, host, program[pid], message) in the files of /var/log and the structured journal read by journalctl hold the same evidence; grep, awk, sort and uniq read them, and the message formats of each program must be known.
                  4. Central collection with a common schema and a 90-day retention makes the entries of all hosts comparable and keeps them when a local log is cleared; seven checks decide whether a log can be trusted.
                  5. A capture is a copy of the frames, taken at a capture point the host does not control (mirror port; promiscuous adapter in the lab), with a capture filter, a snapshot length, bounded files and a capture record; it is targeted, not permanent.
                  6. Read a capture through its summaries: conversations, bytes, timing, services, handshakes, DNS and TLS names. Encrypted content stays hidden; the program and the account come from the host logs.
                  7. Every log and every capture is personal information, and capturing a shared network is interception: Designated Targets only, in the lab, deleted after marking.
                  

                  Terms of the lesson
                  event, log entry, field
                  one recorded occurrence; its written record; one named value inside the record
                  channel
                  one Windows event log (Security, System, Application and the application channels), stored as an .evtx file
                  event number (EventID), record number (EventRecordID)
                  what happened; the position of the entry in its channel, which reveals gaps
                  logon type
                  how an account reached a computer: 2 keyboard, 3 network, 4 batch, 5 service, 7 unlock, 10 remote desktop, 11 cached
                  SubStatus
                  the reason of a failed logon in event 4625, as a hexadecimal code
                  audit policy
                  the Windows settings that decide which Security events are written, for success, failure or both
                  syslog, facility, severity, priority
                  the Linux logging standard (RFC 5424); where a message comes from; how serious it is; facility x 8 + severity
                  rsyslog, journal, journalctl, logrotate
                  the daemon that writes the /var/log files; the structured store of systemd; its reading command; the weekly rotation of the files
                  central collection, retention, normalization, common schema
                  copying entries to a system the hosts cannot modify; how long they are kept; translating them into one fixed list of fields
                  packet, frame, header, payload, encapsulation
                  the unit of transmission; the unit seen on Ethernet; the fixed fields a layer adds in front of its data; the data carried; the nesting of layers
                  capture point, mirror (SPAN) port, TAP, promiscuous mode
                  the interface where frames are copied; the switch feature that copies ports; the inline copying device; the adapter setting that accepts every frame
                  capture filter, display filter
                  what is written to disk (pcap-filter language); what is shown in Wireshark
                  snapshot length (snaplen)
                  the number of bytes kept of each frame; the original length is recorded separately
                  pcap, pcapng
                  the file format of tcpdump (global header and per-frame records); the newer format that Wireshark saves by default
                  conversation, endpoint, top talker
                  the frames exchanged between two endpoints; one address and port; the endpoint with the most bytes
                  three-way handshake, SNI
                  SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, the normal opening of a TCP connection; the server name announced in clear text in the TLS ClientHello
                  flow record
                  one record per connection (addresses, ports, bytes, duration) exported by a firewall or router, without the content
                  capture record
                  the written description of a capture: authorization, operator, time, point, filter, snapshot length, tool, files, hashes, storage and deletion
